_meta.schema: list of {id, label, patterns, match_mode, severity, mitre, why}
_meta.purpose: Layer 3 curated keyword table for core.cmdline_analyzer

match_modes.flag: exact, case-insensitive match against a parsed switch token
match_modes.flag_value: two adjacent tokens — a switch and its value, e.g. '-w hidden'
match_modes.token: exact, case-insensitive match against any parsed token
match_modes.substring: case-insensitive substring of the whole command text; a pattern may also be a LIST of substrings, all of which must appear (in any order or spacing)

_meta.source: briefing §3 Layer 3 seed table, extended against MITRE ATT&CK technique descriptions
notes: Deliberately narrower and more direct than Sigma — this is the fast first pass, not a rule engine.

ids must avoid substrings reserved by ioc.flags.flags_summary_for_evidence (SIGMA, MALWARE, C2, RECON, PERSISTENCE, PRIVESC, LATERAL, SMB, RDP, EXPLOIT, CVE, PHISHING, RANSOMWARE, REGISTRY_MOD, MUTEX, PROCESS_INJECTION, MALWARE_DOWNLOAD, DOWNLOAD_SERVED). Emitted flag ids are CMDLINE_<id>.
'-e' is deliberately absent as an encoded-command alias: too many unrelated tools use it. The deobfuscator still decodes it; only the flag is withheld.
Severities are starting values, not validated against real alert volume — see the known-limits section.

Prefer the list form over a bare binary name. A binary is not a technique: matching 'schtasks' alone labelled a read-only /query as 'Scheduled task created', and 'lsass' alone fired on monitoring tooling that merely names the process. Both were caught by the calibration corpus, not by review.

keywords.label: Base64-encoded command payload
keywords.why: The command body was supplied base64-encoded, a routine way to keep payload content out of logs and out of simple string matching.

keywords.label: Console window hidden from the user
keywords.why: Suppresses the console window so the user sees nothing execute.

keywords.label: PowerShell profile skipped
keywords.why: Skips profile load for a predictable environment. Common in automation too — weak on its own, meaningful alongside other switches.

keywords.label: Non-interactive execution
keywords.why: Suppresses interactive prompts. Benign in scheduled work, notable when paired with hidden windows or encoding.

keywords.label: Execution policy bypassed
keywords.why: Disables the script execution restriction for this invocation.

keywords.label: Arbitrary string executed as code
keywords.why: Executes a string as code — the standard final stage of a fileless dropper.

keywords.label: Fileless download-and-execute cradle
keywords.why: Retrieves remote content directly into memory or disk without a browser.

keywords.label: Inline base64 decoding
keywords.why: Decodes an embedded payload at runtime.

keywords.label: certutil used as a downloader
keywords.why: certutil is a signed Microsoft binary being used to fetch remote content.

keywords.label: BITS used to transfer a file
keywords.why: Background Intelligent Transfer Service moves files while surviving reboots and blending into normal update traffic.

keywords.label: Process spawned through WMI
keywords.why: Creates a process via WMI, detaching it from the normal parent chain.

keywords.label: WMI aimed at a remote host
keywords.why: Executes against another machine — movement between hosts rather than local activity. -ComputerName alone is a read-only query in most cmdlets, so it must be paired with an execution cmdlet.

keywords.label: PsExec-style remote execution
keywords.why: Service-based remote execution tooling.

keywords.label: Copy to or from a network share
keywords.why: Administrative share access, typical of hands-on-keyboard movement.

keywords.label: rundll32 executing script content
keywords.why: A signed binary being used to run inline script, bypassing application control.

keywords.label: mshta fetching remote content
keywords.why: HTML Application host pointed at a remote or scripted payload. The binary alone is not the signal — its target is.

keywords.label: regsvr32 loading a remote scriptlet
keywords.why: The 'squiblydoo' pattern — a signed binary loading a remote COM scriptlet.

keywords.label: Autorun registry key written
keywords.why: Establishes execution at every logon.

keywords.label: Scheduled task created
keywords.why: Scheduled execution. Extremely common in legitimate administration — read alongside what is being scheduled. Requires the creation verb: a read-only /query is not persistence.

keywords.label: Windows service created
keywords.why: Services run as SYSTEM and start automatically.

keywords.label: Known UAC bypass helper binary
keywords.why: Auto-elevating binaries abused to run code at high integrity without a prompt.

keywords.label: LSASS memory access
keywords.why: Reading LSASS memory yields plaintext credentials and hashes. Requires the dumping action, not merely the word lsass — monitoring tooling mentions the process routinely.

keywords.label: Local account created
keywords.why: A new account is a durable foothold that survives cleanup of the original payload.

keywords.label: Account added to administrators
keywords.why: Grants local administrative rights.

keywords.label: Defender configuration tampered with
keywords.why: Disabling protection or excluding a path is a deliberate step to let something else run unimpeded.

keywords.label: AMSI bypass attempt
keywords.why: Neutralises the Antimalware Scan Interface so in-memory content is never inspected. No legitimate use.

keywords.label: ETW telemetry disabled
keywords.why: Blinds Event Tracing for Windows, which most EDR products depend on.

keywords.label: Host firewall turned off
keywords.why: Opens the host to inbound access.

keywords.label: Event log cleared
keywords.why: Destroys the record of what happened. Almost never legitimate on a workstation.

keywords.label: Shell history cleared
keywords.why: Removes the operator's own command history.

keywords.label: Volume shadow copies deleted
keywords.why: Removes local restore points. The standard immediate precursor to ransomware encryption.

keywords.label: Windows recovery disabled
keywords.why: Prevents the host from repairing itself, alongside shadow copy deletion.

keywords.label: Data archived for collection
keywords.why: Bundling files is the staging step before exfiltration.

keywords.label: File marked hidden
keywords.why: Conceals a dropped file from casual inspection.
